content: Household spending grows at fastest rate since mid-2023 “Australians might be telling pollsters they’re doing it tough, but their credit cards clearly haven’t got the memo.” That quote from an investment strategist neatly sums up figures from this morning which show we are in the midst of a surprising and counterintuitive boom in household spending. The Australian Bureau of Statistics showed spending jumped by 1.1% in the month of July (nearly four times as fast as expected), which brought the annual growth rate to 7% – the fastest pace in over three years. The ABS’s monthly release pulls together de-identified card transactions, supermarket scanner data and motor vehicle sales figures. It’s not just we’re being forced to fork out more on groceries and petrol: spending on non-essentials was up an even bigger 7.8% in the year to July as we splurged on clothing and footwear and attended sporting and cultural events. This is all while consumer confidence is in the dumps and real wages go backwards. Part of the increase in spending is explained by higher prices, but Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, admits it’s hard to explain. “It is challenging to unpack, because we are getting mixed signals from a number of different sources,” Allen says. She suspects some of the spending strength in July could be some payback from the initial caution that greeted the start of the Middle East conflict. Maybe Australians are dipping into their savings to spend, and older households have been largely immune to higher interest rates and rents. Whatever explains it, resilient spending adds to bets the Reserve Bank will need to do more to slow the economy if it wants to get inflation back to target. Two men from Western Australia have been charged as part of an alleged cybercrime syndicate authorities say created malicious software to rob thousands of businesses around the globe. The Australian federal police, WA police and the US FBI said in a joint release the men were charged with a combined 14 offences. Police will allege they were part of a “highly organised syndicate” that involved “large-scale cybercrime offending, including data intrusion, identity crime, and cryptocurrency-based money laundering”. Police will allege the syndicate inserted malicious code into software on an open-source platform, which was then used unwittingly by other developers. That infected software was then distributed to computer systems across governments, academia and the private sector which allegedly allowed the syndicate to harvest or steal data. Police allege the code compromised more than 1,000 organisations and enabled the theft of more than 500,000 credentials. The financial impact is expected to be hundreds of millions of dollars in global remediation costs. The men, aged 21 and 23, are scheduled to appear in court today. Glacial collapse caused huge flood leaving hundreds dead or missing in Nepal and Tibet A glacial collapse triggered the catastrophic flash flood in Nepal and Tibet that roared down valleys, wiping out entire villages and leaving a preliminary death toll of at least 165 people, the US Geological Survey said. Rescuers on Thursday raced to locate the hundreds missing, including nationals from India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada. Early reports from Nepali officials initially suggested an earthquake in the area could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4 magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing and the flow of debris. “No earthquake had occurred.” An initial study of Planet Labs satellite imagery indicated that a landslide of ice and rock triggered the debris-laden flood in the Lhende River, about 20km north-east of the Nepal-China Rasuwagadhi border crossing, Nepal’s national disaster authority said. Experts say the risk of such events is compounded by the extreme topography of the Himalayas. Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August, her studio announced in a statement on her website on Thursday. “Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry,” the statement read. She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul. Read more here: Queensland parliament farewells former Labor MP Jimmy Sullivan Queensland parliament has held a condolence motion for the family and friends of former Labor MP Jimmy Sullivan, who died in April. Sullivan followed in the footsteps of his father, Terry, a fellow Stafford MP, who watched on from the public gallery on Thursday as a string of Labor MPs shared their memories. A number of MPs spoke through tears. Many said they’d known Sullivan for decades, at law school, serving as a staffer in the Paluszczuk government or in young Labor. The Labor leader, Steven Miles, told parliament that when they were younger “Jimmy was the one we all agreed would make it”. “While most of the rest of us scrapped our way to get ahead, Jimmy seemed set up,” the former premier said. Charming, funny, smart, popular – he had a way of drawing people to him. The Labor whip, Mark Ryan, called Sullivan “the sentinel of Stafford”, a man who knew people’s names, and whose electorate office was always open. Bundaberg MP Tom Smith said the last time he had spoken to Sullivan, the father-of-two told Smith his child had just learned how to call him “daddy”. “That’s the memory that I want to remember. Jimmy Sullivan, who was proud to be a father, who was so happy
